rewrites.summary:
No Lakshadweep-specific trans statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file; as a union territory without a full legislature its recognition policy is set by the central government, so the recognition machinery facing a visitor or resident runs through the national law.

The national framework narrowed sharply in March 2026: parliament passed an amendment removing the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricting legal recognition to historically recognised communities and intersex people, and requiring medical certification for identity documents and for surgery — a direct documents consequence for a trans traveler. Critics warn many trans and non-binary people will be excluded, a court-appointed advisory panel asked for withdrawal, protests followed the vote, and final assent is pending; whatever the local society, that recognition machinery applies to visitors as it does to residents.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National policy turbulence: the March 2026 amendment passed over warnings from critics and a court-appointed advisory panel that it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people, with protests following the vote, and assent is pending; the human-rights reporting calls the amendment a major reversal of the 2014 rights position, and the change bears uniformly on every state and union territory including this division. No litigation flux or comparison with neighbouring divisions is documented in the dossier for this division.
rewrites.localsOnly: No resident-facing fact specific to Lakshadweep is documented in the dossier; the recognition and certification machinery runs on the national law and governs residents as it governs visitors.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No Lakshadweep-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file, so the assessment rests on the national framework rather than local data. The amendment's operative status is that both houses passed it and final assent is pending, so the controlling legal position for a traveler depends on that unresolved step. No border or entry-paper practice specific to this division beyond the national medical-certification mandate is recorded in the dossier.

rewrites.summary:
No Sikkim-specific trans statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file; the state sits under the national framework, which narrowed sharply in March 2026: parliament removed the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 Supreme Court ruling, restricted recognition to intersex variations and traditional community identities certified by medical boards, and made medical-board certification mandatory for gender-affirming surgery — so identity-document and surgery-authorisation practice for a trans traveler now rests on board certification. A court-appointed advisory panel asked for withdrawal, prominent trans activists warned of mass exclusion, protests followed the vote, and assent is pending.

The framework's enforcement texture nationally includes transit-space 'gender checks': an August 2024 case at a northern railway station, in which a trans traveller alleged a rail-police constable groped her while checking her gender — police denied it and filed a counter-complaint — evidencing a policing habit of treating trans appearance as suspicion in federally policed transit spaces rather than in this state specifically.
rewrites.tangentialFactors: National policy turbulence: the March 2026 amendment passed over warnings from critics and a court-appointed advisory panel that it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people, with protests following the vote, and assent is pending; the human-rights reporting calls the amendment a major reversal of the 2014 rights position, and the change bears uniformly on every state and union territory including this division. No litigation flux or comparison with neighbouring divisions is documented in the dossier for this division.
rewrites.localsOnly: Among the 19 state/UT divisions that have not constituted the transgender welfare board mandated by the 2020 Rules — a documentation/service-delivery gap for residents rather than a visitor-facing signal.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: No Sikkim-specific statute, enforcement series or incident pattern is on file, so the assessment rests on the national framework and the nationally documented policing texture rather than state-level data. The transit-space episode is a single documented complaint that police denied with a counter-complaint, so how the practice operates in this state specifically is unverified. The amendment's operative status is that both houses passed it with assent pending, and no border or entry-paper practice specific to this division beyond the national medical-certification mandate is recorded in the dossier.

rewrites.tangentialFactors: National policy turbulence: the March 2026 amendment passed over warnings from critics and a court-appointed advisory panel that it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people, with protests following the vote, and assent is pending; the human-rights reporting calls the amendment a major reversal of the 2014 rights position, and the change bears uniformly on every state and union territory including this division. No litigation flux or comparison with neighbouring divisions is documented in the dossier for this division.
rewrites.localsOnly: Telangāna has not constituted the transgender welfare board required under the 2020 national rules (one of the 19 state divisions without one); where boards exist they are resident-facing service bodies with no visitor-facing function.
rewrites.outOfScopeNotes: The assessment rests on the country dossier's no-material-deviation finding bounded by the ±0.02 threshold; no division-specific law, enforcement pattern or incident data is on file, and the absence of a deviation signal is not proof of no local practice. The amendment's operative status is that both houses passed it with assent pending, so the controlling legal position for a traveler depends on that unresolved step. No border or entry-paper practice specific to this division beyond the national medical-certification mandate is recorded in the dossier.

blindSourceSummaries: The 2026 trans-rights amendment bill amends the 2019 law: it removes the right to self-identification, limits legal recognition to historically accepted categories and intersex individuals, and mandates medical certification for identity recognition; the international rights organisation calls it a major reversal of the 2014 rights position and urges that final assent not be given (reported 26 March 2026).

Amendment bill approved by both houses (reported 2026, awaiting final assent): removes the self-identification right affirmed by the 2014 'third gender' court ruling; narrows the 2019 definition of transgender person; the government says the narrower definition improves welfare delivery, critics warn it excludes trans men, trans women, non-binary and gender-fluid people; mandatory medical certification described as an attack on privacy and dignity.
